title: Can social media videos help reduce stigma towards people with psoriasis? A study with young men in the UK
official: A Solomon-four-group randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of co-produced social media influencer video content on stigmatising attitudes towards people with psoriasis among males aged 18-27 years in the UK
summary:
Background and study aims
Psoriasis is a common long-term skin condition that can cause visible changes to the skin. People living with psoriasis can experience negative reactions from other people, including staring, avoidance, incorrect assumptions and negative stereotypes. These experiences are often described as psoriasis-related stigma and can have an important impact on wellbeing and quality of life.

Social media is an increasingly important source of health information, particularly for younger adults. It may also provide an opportunity for people with health conditions to share their experiences directly with others. However, there is currently limited evidence about whether social media content featuring people living with psoriasis can help improve public understanding and reduce negative attitudes.

This study aims to investigate whether short social media-style videos, developed together with people affected by psoriasis, can influence attitudes and understanding towards people living with psoriasis among young men in the UK.

Who can participate?
The study is open to males aged 18 to 27 years who currently live in the UK.

Participants will need to be able to understand written and spoken English and have access to an internet-connected device that can play short videos and complete an online questionnaire.

What does the study involve?
The study is completed entirely online. Participants will first read information about the research and provide informed consent if they wish to take part. They will then answer some questions about themselves and their previous experiences and familiarity with skin conditions.

Participants will be randomly allocated to one of several study groups. Neither the participant nor the researcher chooses which group they enter. Depending on the group they are allocated to, participants may complete some questions before viewing the videos. All participants will then watch six short social media-style videos. The exact video content shown will depend on which group they have been randomly allocated to.

After watching the videos, participants will complete questionnaires about their views, attitudes and responses towards people living with psoriasis. These will include questions about beliefs about psoriasis and willingness to interact with someone with psoriasis. Participants may also be shown photographs and asked for their responses to them. Some questions may appear similar at different points in the study. This is intentional and is an important part of the research design. The whole study is expected to take approximately 30–40 minutes to complete.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There may be no direct personal benefit from taking part. However, the findings may help researchers understand whether social media content could be used to improve public understanding of psoriasis and reduce stigma towards people living with the condition. This may help inform the development of future public education and awareness interventions.

The study involves viewing images and videos relating to psoriasis and answering questions about attitudes towards people with visible skin conditions. Some participants may find discussion or images of visible skin conditions uncomfortable. Some questions also ask participants to report their opinions honestly, including opinions that may be considered negative.

Participants do not have to provide an answer where the questionnaire allows them to move on, and they can stop taking part by closing their browser before completing and submitting the study. Information about support and relevant organisations will be provided at the end of the study. There are no known physical risks associated with taking part.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being run by researchers at the Centre for Appearance Research at the University of the West of England (UWE Bristol), UK. Participation takes place entirely online, so participants can take part from anywhere in the UK using a suitable internet-connected device.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study is expected to begin recruiting participants in October 2026. Recruitment and data collection are expected to take place over approximately 2-3 week window period, with the wider research project continuing while the findings are analysed and reported.

Who is funding the study?
The research forms part of a PhD project funded by Psoriasis UK (formally the Psoriasis Association).
